## [Internationalization (i18n)](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/i18n/) (I18n)

---
title: "Internationalization (i18n)"
description: "Translation catalogs, the gen_i18n.py generator, ownership rules, and what the merge validates."
---

# Internationalization (i18n)

The SDK carries the translation engine, the generator tooling, and the base catalog of SDK-owned strings. An app brings its own catalog. At build time the catalogs merge into a single enum and one set of string tables per firmware image.

## Layout

```text
PocketMage_SDK/
  pocketmage_i18n/
    pocketmage_i18n.h / .cpp          # runtime engine (I18n class)
    languages/                        # base catalog (SDK-owned strings)
      en/pocketmage_i18n.po
      fr/pocketmage_i18n.po
      fr/pocketmage_i18n.aliases
      es/...  de/...
    tools/
      gen_i18n.py                     # merger, generator, and build hook
    tests/
      test_gen_i18n.py
```

An app adds one catalog directory of its own:

```text
<app>/src/i18n/
  en/pocketmage_i18n.po
  fr/pocketmage_i18n.po
  fr/pocketmage_i18n.aliases
  ...
```

A catalog directory has one subdirectory per language, named by the language code. `en` is required and defines that catalog's string order.

## Catalog format

Standard gettext `.po`. `msgctxt` is the `StringID` enum name; `msgid` is the English text; `msgstr` is the translation. The `en` file carries a `# Languages:` directive in its leading comment block:

```po
# PocketMage OS English Translations
# Languages: en fr es de

msgctxt "STR_SYS_HELLO"
msgid "Hello"
msgstr "Hello"
```

That directive, in the base catalog, is where the language list and order come from. Each catalog's `en` file defines the order of the strings that catalog contributes; the catalog's other languages must list the same `msgctxt`s, with the same `msgid`s, in the same order.

A language missing from a catalog falls back to that catalog's English text, so an English-only app catalog is valid without translating anything.

### Aliases

`pocketmage_i18n.aliases` maps folded, lowercase user input to a `StringID`. Optional, only defined for non-English languages:

```text
annuler -> STR_KB_APP_CANCEL
```

Folding strips diacritics (`Paramètres -> parametres`). Aliases from all catalogs concatenate per language; a key that folds to the same value twice is a build error.

## Ownership

| Owner            | Namespaces                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| SDK base catalog | `STR_KB_*` (incl. `STR_KB_APP_*`, `STR_KB_USB_*`, `STR_KB_INIT_*`), `STR_GRID_*`, `STR_SD_*`, `STR_WIFI_*`, `STR_SYS_*`, `STR_TOUCHPAD_*`, `STR_OLED_*`, `STR_FRAME(S)_*`, `STR_INFO/GOOD/SAVED_*`, `STR_DAY_*`, `STR_MONTH_*`                                  |
| App catalog      | `STR_TERM_*`, `STR_ONBOARD_*`, `STR_SSH_*`, `STR_SETTINGS_*`, `STR_CAL_*`, `STR_UTILS_*`, `STR_LOCK_*`, `STR_HOME_*`, `STR_TASKS_*`, `STR_FILEWIZ_*`, `STR_APPLOADER_*`, `STR_COMM_*`, `STR_USB_*`, `STR_LEX_*`, `STR_JOURNAL_*`, `STR_TXT_*`, `STR_GOTO_*`, `STR_SAVE_*` |

`msgctxt` names are globally unique across the merged catalogs; reusing one the SDK already defines is a build error. SDK code only references SDK namespaces, so merging an app catalog never changes how SDK code behaves.

Ownership follows the consumer: base if SDK code references the string, app otherwise. That keeps a bare SDK checkout building standalone (its base catalog contains every string its own modules use), and the merge appends the app catalog after the base, so app strings never move base enum values. The indexed helper ranges all sit in the base; their relative order is fixed and never perturbed by an app catalog.

## Generator

`tools/gen_i18n.py` merges the catalogs in command-line order and writes `pocketmage_i18n_gen.h` and `pocketmage_i18n_gen.cpp`:

```sh
python3 pocketmage_i18n/tools/gen_i18n.py \
    --catalog pocketmage_i18n/languages \
    --catalog ../app/src/i18n \
    --out-dir <build-dir>
```

`--catalog` is repeatable; the first catalog is the base. With no arguments, the tool generates the SDK's own base catalog into `pocketmage_i18n/`, so a bare SDK checkout builds standalone.

The merge keeps base strings first and appends each later catalog in turn. Every enum value equals its index in the merged order, so the layout is stable: adding an app catalog never changes SDK string values.

### Validation

The generator exits non-zero and aborts the build on any of:

- a missing `# Languages:` directive in the base `en` file, or `en` not first;
- a `msgctxt` that is not `[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*`;
- a duplicate `msgctxt` within a catalog or across catalogs;
- a non-`en` file whose `msgctxt` set, order, or `msgid`s differ from that catalog's `en`;
- a duplicated folded alias;
- the indexed helper ranges missing, inverted, overlapping, or out of order.

### Indexed helper ranges

Four ranges are indexed by the runtime helpers (`appName()`, `dayName()`, `monthName()`, `kbAppName()`). They must stay contiguous blocks, in this order:

| Range                                      | Members                               |
| ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `STR_KB_APP_CANCEL` .. `STR_KB_APP_LOADER` | app list in the keyboard app switcher |
| `STR_GRID_TXT` .. `STR_GRID_LOADER`        | app list in the launcher grid         |
| `STR_DAY_SUNDAY` .. `STR_DAY_SATURDAY`     | weekdays                              |
| `STR_MONTH_JAN` .. `STR_MONTH_ERR`         | months (`ERR` is the last member)     |

Their heads are emitted with explicit `= N` enum values as documentation of intent; the values always equal the index in the merged order.

## Build integration

The generator doubles as the build hook. Point `extra_scripts` at it in the app's `platformio.ini`; it reads its settings from project options (or `POCKETMAGE_I18N_CATALOGS` / `POCKETMAGE_I18N_OUT_DIR`, or the SDK base catalog as a last resort):

```ini
extra_scripts = pre:lib/PocketMage_SDK/pocketmage_i18n/tools/gen_i18n.py

custom_i18n_catalogs =
    lib/PocketMage_SDK/pocketmage_i18n/languages
    src/i18n
custom_i18n_out_dir = .pio/build/${PIOENV}/i18n
```

As a hook it regenerates only when a `.po`/`.aliases` file is newer than the generated tables, so incremental builds stay cheap.

`custom_i18n_out_dir` must be ahead of any stale copy on the include path. The engine includes `"pocketmage_i18n_gen.h"`; the generated files are build artifacts, never committed.

## Adding a string or a language

- **String:** add the `msgctxt`/`msgid`/`msgstr` to the owning catalog's `en` file and to each language file, in the same position relative to that catalog's other strings. App strings go in the app catalog.
- **Language:** append the code to the base `en` file's `# Languages:` directive and add that language's directory to each catalog that translates it. Never reorder existing languages: the index is the value stored in NVS.

## Testing

```sh
python3 -m unittest discover -s pocketmage_i18n/tests
```

The suite covers catalog merging, language fallback, alias merging, and every validation failure above, using small in-test catalogs.

There is no firmware reflash: you build an ELF, pack it with an overlay sidecar and an icon, copy the tar onto the SD card, and install it through the on-device app loader. These docs cover the whole path, from installing the toolchain to the binary contract the loader enforces.

## Start here

::: steps

1. Install the toolchain: [Get Started](get-started/toolchain.md).
2. Build your first app end to end: [Your first app](get-started/first-app.md).
3. Learn the model: [Making an app](guides/making-apps.md), then the [API overview](api/index.md).
4. Read the contract: [App ABI](app-abi.md) and [Overlay format](overlay.md).
5. Check what your app resolves against: [Symbols](symbols.md).
6. Ship a tar: [Publishing](guides/publishing.md).
7. Port existing code: [Migration](migration.md).

## [Migrating an existing app](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/migration/) (Migration)

---
title: "Migrating an existing app"
description: "Moving a pre-ELF app to the runtime-load flow: what changed, the eight steps, and the traps that bite."
---

# Migrating an existing app

Production devices no longer run apps built the old way. An app is now a runtime-loaded ELF shipped as `/apps/*.tar`; there is no firmware-flashing app flow and no OTA-style app package on production.

The short version: if you shipped an app pre-ELF, that package will not launch on production firmware. Rebuild it against the ELF contract and re-package.

## What changed

| Aspect          | Old flow                                   | New flow                                             |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Binary          | monolithic app inside the firmware image   | standalone `ET_DYN` ELF                            |
| Delivery        | firmware `.bin` / OTA-style app package    | `/apps/<name>.tar` on the SD card, installed via APPLOADER |
| Instantiation   | compiled in, launched by the OS            | loaded in-process when launched, torn down on return |
| Dependencies    | linked into the firmware build             | resolved from the host at load time (`-nostdlib`)    |
| Toolchain       | PlatformIO (big-endian)                    | espressif `xtensa-esp-elf`                          |
| Layout/naming   | app id / metadata                          | derived from the tar base name                       |

The OS keeps app code out of PSRAM by design; code runs from IRAM. That is the loader's job, not yours.

## Migration steps

1. **Get the toolchain.** Install the espressif `xtensa-esp-elf` toolchain into `~/.espressif/...` as shown in [build.md](build.md). Do not rely on the PlatformIO toolchain; it emits big-endian ELFs the loader cannot read.
2. **Scaffold.** Run `pm new myapp`. Its `Makefile` (`include tools/app.mk`) is the whole build system.
3. **Port the entry.** Wrap your start logic in `extern "C" int main(int, char**)`. The build renames it to `app_main`. Fit the previous app's lifetime to the return-from-`main` model ([app-abi.md](app-abi.md)).
4. **Replace dependencies.** Every call must resolve at load time. Host exports are the curated surface in [symbols.md](symbols.md) plus the host's newlib/IDF/Arduino globals. That covers display, keyboard, buzzer, clock, IO, and the standard library. If you depended on app-side firmware globals that are not exported, move that dependency to API calls.
5. **Move assets.** Files the app used at compile time become a top-level `assets/` directory in the tar, read at runtime from `/assets/<name>` ([publishing](guides/publishing.md)).
6. **Localize.** If the app contained strings, move them into an app catalog (`src/i18n/`, merged per [i18n.md](i18n.md)) instead of hardcoding.
7. **Verify.** `make clean all check` must succeed, list a sane set of undefined symbols, and the endianness check must pass. Then `make pack` and `tar -tvf build/<name>.tar`.
8. **Ship.** Copy the tar to `/apps/` on the device, install with APPLOADER into a slot, launch. The launcher shows the name and icon drawn from the package.

## Gotchas

- **Big-endian artifacts.** The classic failure. The loader does no byte swapping, so a PlatformIO-built app faults at load with a section or instruction fault. `readelf -h` shows `big endian` before you ship.
- **Statically linked runtime.** Symbols collide or bloat; keep `-nostdlib`.
- **Relying on slot directories.** After install the ELF lives in the slot dir, but the app should treat `/assets/<name>` (copied at install) as its data home and never assume the slot path.
- **Long-lived loops.** The app shares the device. Cooperative lifetimes (render, yield via the SDK API, return) beat spin loops on the 16 KB run stack.

## Announcement

If you maintained published apps pre-ELF, publish a migration notice: existing packages targeting production will not launch on the new firmware, and step 8 above is the path forward.

---

## [Overlay format (.elfo)](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/overlay/) (Overlay)

---
title: "Overlay format (.elfo)"
description: "The ELFO overlay blob that ships beside every app ELF: why it exists, its on-disk layout, and how the host pages overlay bodies into executable RAM."
---

# Overlay format (`.elfo`)

Every packed app carries two artifacts: the relocatable `<name>.app.elf` and a sidecar `<name>.elfo`. The ELF is the program; the ELFO blob is the overlay image the host pages into executable RAM at load time. The build produces the `.elfo` automatically (see [build.md](build.md)); this page documents what it contains and how the loader consumes it, so the format is pinned contract rather than an implementation detail.

The overlay runtime lives in the `elf_overlay` component, an ISA-abstracted overlay loader that sits next to the ELF loader (`esp_elf`) and handles the parts of loading that a plain relocating loader cannot: paging `.text` bodies into a fixed pool of executable frames and patching ISA-specific PC-relative literal loads once the resident addresses are known.

## Why it exists

An ELF app links `-nostdlib -shared` and resolves every symbol from the host at load time (see [app-abi.md](app-abi.md) and [symbols.md](symbols.md)). On the ESP32-S3 the loader must place executable code in memory that the instruction bus can fetch (`MALLOC_CAP_EXEC`), which is scarce. Mapping an entire app image into exec RAM wastes that budget on code paths that may never run.

The overlay model solves this. Instead of loading all `.text` up front, the host relocates the base image with `esp_elf`, then pages individual overlay bodies into a small pool of exec-RAM frames on demand. A function that is never called is never paged in. The `.elfo` blob is the pre-chewed form the device needs for that: the overlay bodies, the stub block that enters and leaves them, and the relocation patch tables the host applies once it knows where each frame landed.

PC-relative literal loads (`l32r` on Xtensa, `auipc` on RISC-V) cannot be left to the base relocator, because the literal's absolute address is not known until the overlay body is resident. `elf_overlay` patches those in place at page-in. The base relocator never touches them.

## On-disk layout

The blob begins with the four-byte magic `ELFO`, format version 1, and an ISA tag. All multi-byte fields are little-endian, matching the app ELF. The header is followed by fixed-shape tables and two data regions:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    H["elf_overlay_header_t<br>magic ELFO, version, ISA tag, table counts"]
    O["overlay entries<br>id, offset, length (one per overlay body)"]
    S["stub entries<br>canonical vaddr, overlay_id, body_offset, stub_off"]
    R["redirect entries<br>call site, stub_off"]
    P["patch entries<br>overlay_id, blob_offset, insn_offset"]
    SP["stub_patch entries<br>overlay_id, blob_offset, insn_offset"]
    HR["host_ref entries<br>overlay_id, blob_offset, insn_offset, name_off"]
    ST["string table<br>null-terminated host symbol names"]
    SB["stub block<br>enter/leave slots plus stub code"]
    B["overlay bodies<br>verbatim .text images"]
    H --> O --> S --> R --> P --> SP --> HR --> ST --> SB --> B
```

| Table        | What it records                                                         |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| overlay      | Each overlay body's id, its offset into the bodies region, and length.  |
| stub         | Maps a canonical `.text` virtual address to the stub that enters it.    |
| redirect     | Resident call sites that must be patched to jump through a stub.        |
| patch        | ISA literal-load sites inside overlay bodies, patched at page-in.       |
| stub_patch   | ISA literal-load sites inside the stub block.                           |
| host_ref     | Overlay references to host symbols, resolved by name via the resolver.  |
| string table | The host symbol names the `host_ref` entries point into.                |

All tables are fixed-size records, so parsing and page-in do no heap allocation beyond the frame pool itself.

## ISA abstraction

ISA-specific patching lives behind `elf_overlay_isa_ops_t`. Two backends are registered:

- `xtensa` - `l32r` PC-relative literal patching, validated against the Xtensa ISA reference. This is the backend PocketMage uses on the S3.
- `riscv` - `auipc` PC-relative literal patching.

The ISA tag in the header selects the backend at load time. A blob built for one ISA will not load on another.

## How the host consumes it

The in-process runner (`src/elf_runner.cpp`) loads an app in two stages: the base relocation with `esp_elf`, then the overlay with `elf_overlay`. The exact sequence, matching the code:

1. Install the scoped symbol resolver (see [symbols.md](symbols.md)), then `esp_elf_init` and `esp_elf_relocate_source` relocate the base image. The image is streamed by offset from the SD file rather than held whole in RAM.
2. Locate the `.elfo` sidecar next to the ELF and `elf_overlay_load` it.
3. `elf_overlay_set_active` makes it the active overlay for the run.
4. `elf_overlay_esp_elf_set_section_map` copies the relocated section table (canonical virtual address to resident address) from the `esp_elf_t` into the overlay's section map.
5. `elf_overlay_apply_redirects` patches the resident call sites so calls into paged functions go through their stubs.
6. `elf_overlay_set_symbol_resolver` wires host-reference resolution back through the scoped resolver, so an overlay body calling a `pm_*` or runtime symbol resolves against the host export table.
7. The entry point is redirected: the runner finds the stub for the entry's canonical virtual address and rewrites `elf.entry` to the stub address, so even the first call pages the entry body in.
8. `esp_elf_request` runs the entry. On return, the overlay is unloaded and the base image deinitialized.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as elf_runner
    participant E as esp_elf
    participant O as elf_overlay
    participant SD as SD card
    R->>R: install scoped symbol resolver
    R->>E: esp_elf_init
    E->>SD: esp_elf_relocate_source (stream by offset)
    R->>SD: locate name.elfo sidecar
    R->>O: elf_overlay_load
    R->>O: elf_overlay_set_active
    E-->>O: elf_overlay_esp_elf_set_section_map (section table)
    R->>O: elf_overlay_apply_redirects (patch call sites)
    R->>O: elf_overlay_set_symbol_resolver (host refs)
    R->>O: redirect elf.entry to entry stub
    R->>E: esp_elf_request (run entry)
    E-->>R: entry returns
    R->>O: elf_overlay unload
    R->>E: esp_elf deinit
```

If the sidecar is absent, the app runs unredirected from the base relocation alone. Apps packed with `make pack` always ship the sidecar; see the pack contract in [publishing](guides/publishing.md).

### The frame pool

A fixed pool of executable-RAM frames holds overlay bodies, paged in on demand. A stub's `enter` bumps the target frame's refcount and `leave` drops it; a frame stays resident while its refcount is above zero. Literals are patched in place inside the `.text` image at page-in, once resident addresses are known. The PC-relative instructions themselves (`l32r` / `auipc`) are never rewritten.

The pool is sized by compile-time constants in the overlay component (`ELF_OVERLAY_MAX_FRAMES`, default 4; `ELF_OVERLAY_DEFAULT_FRAME_SIZE`, default 16384 bytes). A single overlay body must fit in one frame.

## Building the blob

`tools/app.mk` emits the `.elfo` in two steps from the unstripped link output (`<name>.app.tool`):

```text
elf_overlay_relink <name>.app.tool <name>.relk   # scan .text, classify relocs
elf_overlay_emit   <name>.relk     <name>.elfo   # pack into the ELFO blob
```

`elf_overlay_relink` reads the ELF32 executable, scans `.text` for ISA patch sites, builds a literal pool, classifies relocations, and writes a `.relk` intermediate. `elf_overlay_emit` packs that into the final ELFO blob. Both tools must be on `PATH`; the SDK build expects them from an `elf_overlay` checkout (CI builds them with CMake and prepends the build dir to `PATH`). Override `ELF_OVERLAY_RELINK` and `ELF_OVERLAY_EMIT` to point at specific binaries.

## Stability

The ELFO magic, version, and table layout are load contract. A format change takes a version bump in the header and a matching host loader that accepts the new version. The `elf_overlay` component is the single source of truth for the format; see its `README.md` and `include/elf_overlay/` headers for the exact record definitions.

## [Symbols and the dependency contract](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/symbols/) (Symbols)

---
title: "Symbols and the dependency contract"
description: "The host-export surface apps resolve against, how third-party libraries link, and the rules for changing the surface."
---

# Symbols and the dependency contract

Apps link `-nostdlib`. Nothing ships with the binary that satisfies a reference; at load time the host resolves every undefined symbol from its own live memory. The app's undefined-symbol list is therefore its real dependency contract. `make check` prints it; `pm check` interprets it against the host surface.

## The surface

An app can call anything the host exports as a global symbol. The export surface has two curated parts, backed by two committed lists at the SDK root:

- `symbols.list` - the PocketMage `pm_*` ABI plus a handful of host primitives. Its `pm_*` block is generated; do not hand edit it (see below).
- `host_baseline.list` - the C/C++ runtime, newlib, and POSIX symbols the firmware exports unconditionally. Apps may rely on these without listing them. Generated from the firmware's export table; do not hand edit it.

The `pm` gate reads both lists and takes their union as the curated surface (`tools/pm/gate.py:read_curated`). An undefined symbol in an app must appear in that union, or be confirmed present in a supplied host ELF, for the app to pass.

**The C and C++ runtime.** `libc`, `libm`, `libgcc`, `libstdc++` and `libsupc++` symbols the firmware already links are exported so apps can use third-party libraries, and `host_baseline.list` records them. `tools/symbols.py` derives this set by reading the toolchain archives with `nm` and keeping the symbols that are present in the firmware image:

```sh
python3 tools/symbols.py --list symbols.list --host-elf <firmware.elf> \
  --print-cost
```

```
libc        250 symbols   4,467 bytes
libm         15 symbols     262 bytes
libstdc++    87 symbols   3,403 bytes
libsupc++    58 symbols   2,362 bytes
libgcc       65 symbols   1,552 bytes
libnewlib    94 symbols   2,478 bytes
total       602 symbols  15,009 bytes (14.7 KB)
```

That total includes the curated `pm_*` entries. The runtime adds about 11.2 KB of flash in the firmware image, once. It is not a per-app cost. Apps stay small: a hello world is 1.3 KB, an app using `std::vector` and `std::string` is 2.3 KB, an app with cJSON linked in is 5.2 KB. `--gc-sections` and `--strip-all` in `tools/app.mk` do that work.

A symbol in `symbols.list` that the firmware does not define is reported as a warning but still emitted into the table. A newly added wrapper cannot appear in `--host-elf` until the host is rebuilt, so dropping it would omit it on the one run that adds it. Regenerate once more after building and the warning should be gone.

Runtime export is on by default. Pass `--no-runtime` to export only the curated SDK list, which restricts apps to the SDK surface and no libraries.

Membership is decided by which archive a symbol comes from, not by its name. A `_ZN...` prefix also matches the SDK's own C++ classes, so matching on prefix shape would export firmware internals by accident.

GCC reserves `__atomic_*`, `__sync_*` and `__builtin_*` names as builtins and rejects taking their address. Those exports are declared under a private `pm_elfsym_` identifier with an asm label, then listed by their literal name in the table.

**The curated SDK table.** `symbols.list` is PocketMage's own export promise. Its `pm_*` block is generated by `tools/gen_app_api.py`, which walks the SDK headers, projects each C++ method to a C wrapper, and writes the wrapper names into both `symbols.list` (SDK side) and `src/ELF_SYMS/host_exports.list` (OS side) so the two can never drift. `tools/symbols.py` is a different tool: it derives the runtime baseline above from the toolchain archives. Host-side, `host_exports.list` tracks a superset of `symbols.list`, validated against the firmware image. Both lists feed the same generated `g_customer_elfsyms` table.

Do not hand edit the `pm_*` block of `symbols.list`. To change the app-facing surface, change the SDK header and regenerate with `gen_app_api.py`; it rewrites the generated files together.

## Linking a third-party library

A vendored library's source is compiled into the app by overriding `APP_SRCS`. Anything the library references that is not in the app is resolved by the host at load time. Two consequences are worth knowing.

Libraries compiled at `-Os` need fewer symbols than the same source at `-O0`. A `std::vector<std::string>` app at `-O0` wants 13 symbols including `std::allocator<char>` constructors; at `-Os` it wants 7, and all 7 resolve.

`sscanf` is not exported by default. It exists in newlib, but nothing in the firmware references it, so it was dropped by `--gc-sections`, and referencing it pulls in about 190 KB of stdio reentrancy. A library that needs it must either avoid it or the host must export it deliberately.

## Reading an app's contract

```sh
make check   # prints entry + every undefined symbol
pm check     # classifies each symbol and exits non-zero on a broken contract
```

Everything in that list must exist in the host's global view when the app loads, or the load fails. `pm check` with `--host-elf` is the exact gate: every undefined symbol must resolve to a host global.

Without a host ELF, `pm check` reads the generated export table that the firmware links, which is the same file the loader searches. It does not keep a separate allowlist, because a hand-written list drifts from the table and the drift shows up only on device. An earlier allowlist claimed `memmove` and `sprintf` were resolvable when no table exported them, so those apps passed the gate and failed at load with `Can't find common memmove`. Reading the generated table makes that class of bug impossible.

## Editing the surface

Rules for SDK authors:

- Additions only. Removing or renaming an exported symbol breaks every app that references it at runtime.
- Every added SDK symbol must exist as a `GLOBAL` in the firmware image and be added to both `symbols.list` and the host's `host_exports.list`, then regenerate the host table with `tools/symbols.py --host-elf ...`.
- Regenerate the host table whenever the firmware's linked symbol set changes. `symbols.py` only exports runtime symbols the firmware already links, so a firmware that starts using a new libc or libstdc++ function makes it available on the next regeneration.
- Run `pm exports` before committing a surface change. It reconciles `symbols.list` against `host_exports.list` and fails when a curated symbol is not exported.
- Bump `pocketmage_sdk_version` when the surface changes. It is exported, and stored so the OS can version apps against the surface.

Exporting a broad slice of the firmware binds the ABI to all of it. That is a deliberate trade here: it is what lets apps use libraries.

## Per-app scope

The broad surface is the default, but an app can be narrowed to a subset of the `pm_*` surface through the `scope` field in its `app.properties` manifest (default `all`). At load time the runner parses the scope and installs a scoped resolver: a `pm_*` symbol outside the app's scope resolves to nothing, so the load fails fast with `ELF needs symbols outside its scope` rather than letting the app reach an API it did not declare. Only `pm_*` symbols are gated; the runtime baseline (libc, libstdc++, ESP-IDF) stays reachable for any scope, so libraries keep working. See [app-abi.md](app-abi.md) for the manifest fields and the runner's resolver behavior.

## Versioning and gating

`pocketmage_sdk_version` is exported so apps can adapt to surface changes. `pm check` gates an app against the host export set before release: the mirror of `make check`, with the generated table as the reference when no host ELF is available.

Ship a new version with `pm release <major|minor|patch>` (add `--message TEXT` for a CHANGELOG bullet). It validates VERSION, the `pocketmage_sdk_version` literal in `pocketmage_globals.cpp`, `pocketmage_app_version.h`, and `library.json` first, then rewrites all four and folds an `[N.N.N]` header at the top of `CHANGELOG.md`. No write happens if any file disagrees. The command stages nothing in git; commit the four files and the changelog together.

## [Troubleshooting](https://talismandesign.github.io/PocketMage_SDK/docs/troubleshooting/) (Troubleshooting)

---
title: "Troubleshooting"
description: "The failures an app build or load hits most, what causes each, and how to fix it."
---

# Troubleshooting

The failure modes below are the ones an app build or load actually hits. Each entry names the symptom, the cause, and the fix. The deeper references are linked from each.

## Build and toolchain

### `XTENSA_CXX` not found, or the wrong compiler is used

The build probes for the espressif `xtensa-esp32s3-elf-g++` and falls back to the PlatformIO package and `PATH`. If it picks the PlatformIO package, the link output has the wrong byte order and the endianness guard deletes it (see below). Pin the compiler explicitly:

```sh
make XTENSA_CXX=~/.espressif/tools/xtensa-esp-elf/esp-15.2.0_20251204/xtensa-esp-elf/bin/xtensa-esp32s3-elf-g++
```

Confirm what the build resolved with `make pm-info`. The install steps are in [toolchain.md](get-started/toolchain.md).

### The build fails with an endianness assertion and deletes the artifact

`app.mk` asserts little-endian output after every link and removes a big-endian artifact so a bad file never ships. This almost always means the wrong toolchain compiled the app. Only the espressif `xtensa-esp-elf` toolchain emits readable output; the PlatformIO Xtensa package does not. Fix the toolchain, not the guard.

### `elf_overlay_relink` or `elf_overlay_emit` not found

The `.elfo` overlay sidecar is built by two host tools that must be on `PATH`. Build them from an `elf_overlay` checkout and add the build directory to `PATH`, or point `ELF_OVERLAY_RELINK` and `ELF_OVERLAY_EMIT` at the binaries. See [toolchain.md](get-started/toolchain.md#install-the-toolchain-elfoverlay-host-tools).

### A single function will not fit in an overlay frame

An overlay body must fit in one frame of the executable-RAM pool (`ELF_OVERLAY_DEFAULT_FRAME_SIZE`, default 16 KB). A single function larger than a frame cannot be paged in. Split the function. See [overlay.md](overlay.md#overlay-format-elfo-how-the-host-consumes-it-the-frame-pool).

## Gating (`pm check`)

### Symbols reported as "broken" / "not resolvable by the host"

The app references a symbol the host does not export. The load would fail. The symbol must be added to the SDK's curated surface before an app can use it, or the app must stop referencing it. The symbol model is in [symbols.md](symbols.md).

### Symbols reported as "unconfirmed"

The symbol sits outside the curated surface (`symbols.list` plus `host_baseline.list`), so `pm check` cannot confirm it without the actual host export table. Re-run with `--host-elf <firmware.elf>` for an exact result.

### Warning: `app_main` is not in the ELF's symbol table

Not a failure. The post-link strip removed the `app_main` name, but the entry is linker-pinned with `-e app_main`, so the loader still finds it. Ignore it.

### Warning: the app has a non-empty `.init_array`

The app links static constructors. The host's `esp_elf` loader does not run relocation-time constructors, so they never execute. Remove the static construction, or move the initialization into `app_main`. The compile flags `-fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics` are on by default to keep this from happening; a remaining `.init_array` usually comes from a global with a non-trivial constructor. See [app-abi.md](app-abi.md#app-binary-contract-abi-how-loading-works).

## pm tooling

### `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tools'` when running `pm`

The `pm` command was installed editable (`pip install -e`) against a checkout that has since moved or been deleted, so its link to the `tools` package is dead. A common trigger is installing from a temporary scaffold directory that the OS later cleaned up. Current `pm` builds detect this and offer to reinstall; if you see the raw error, the installed CLI predates the resilient launcher. Reinstall against a live checkout:

```sh
pm update-sdk --sdk /path/to/PocketMage_SDK
```

If `pm` itself will not start, run the equivalent reinstall directly with the interpreter that owns the `pm` script:

```sh
/path/to/that/python -m pip install -e /path/to/PocketMage_SDK
```

Run [`pm doctor`](cli.md#pm-cli-commands-pm-doctor) afterward to confirm the install is healthy.

### `pm` behaves differently from the SDK checkout you are editing

The installed CLI is a different version from the checkout. `pm doctor` reports the version skew. Reinstall to re-sync:

```sh
pm update-sdk
```

An editable install avoids this in the first place, because the CLI tracks the checkout it was linked to. See [the install notes](cli.md#pm-cli-install).

## Load-time (on device)

### `ELF needs symbols outside its scope`

The app's `app.properties` manifest declares a `scope` that does not include a `pm_*` symbol the app actually calls, so the scoped resolver refuses to resolve it and the load fails fast. Widen the `scope` (default `all`) to cover the API the app uses, or stop calling the out-of-scope API. Only `pm_*` symbols are gated by scope; the runtime baseline is always reachable. See [symbols.md](symbols.md#symbols-and-the-dependency-contract-per-app-scope).

### The app loads but runs unredirected / behaves oddly on large code paths

The `.elfo` sidecar was not found next to the ELF, so the app ran from the base relocation alone without the overlay. Confirm the tar shipped the `.elfo` member (`tar -tf build/<name>.tar`) and that the installer placed it in the slot. See [overlay.md](overlay.md#overlay-format-elfo-how-the-host-consumes-it).

### The app never returns control

Returning from `app_main` is how an app exits: the overlay is unloaded, the base image deinitialized, and HOME reopens. An app that never returns leaks the run task. A UI app must hand control back cooperatively and then return. See [app-abi.md](app-abi.md#app-binary-contract-abi-entry-point).

## Packaging and install

### The device will not install the tar

The installer only accepts a plain `.tar` in `/apps`, not a gzip, not a loose directory, not a `.bin`. It keys off the first `*.app.elf` member. Rebuild with `make pack` (or `pm pack`), which produces the correct shape, and verify with `tar -tvf`. See [publishing](guides/publishing.md).

### macOS `._*` junk in the package

Creating the tar from Finder copies pulls in `._*` metadata files. The installer skips them, but they bloat the package. `make pack` avoids them; use it rather than tarring by hand.
